dialogue.text: That's a tricky question. We can be aware of our own experiences, but the gap between minds seems inherent to the human condition.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Right, but some philosophers argue that consciousness might arise from purely physical processes in the brain. How do you see that?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I find that somewhat plausible, but it depends on the frame you use. If you assume a purely materialist frame, then yes, but that assumption might be too limiting.

dialogue.speaker: A

dialogue.translation: Kasi ozali koloba ete ndenge tozali kobakisa makasi ezali kobimisa oyo tozali koyeba? Yango ezali kobimisa makasi ya ntina, eh?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Exactly. And there's also the question of whether consciousness has a unique dimension beyond the physical. Some call it the 'hard problem'.
dialogue.translation: Kaka. Kasi ezali mibeko mpo na koyeba soki makasi ezali na makasi ya makasi ya makasi. Bato mosusu bazali koloba ete 'mibeko ya makasi'.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: But if that dimension exists, how would we ever measure it? Science relies on observable data, whereby we infer mental states from behavior.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: True, but our capacity to observe is limited. Even in humans, we can't directly access another's subjective experience.
dialogue.translation: Kasi makasi na biso ya kozua ezali ya makasi. Ata na bato, tozali kozua te makasi ya makasi ya mosusu.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: So maybe consciousness will always remain a mystery in some sense. But that doesn't stop us from exploring it, does it?

dialogue.speaker: A

dialogue.speaker: B
